planting.note: Direct sow a couple of weeks before to a couple of weeks after the last frost; Titicaca was bred in Denmark for day-length neutrality and reaches maturity far faster than most quinoa lines, making it one of the more reliable choices for short, cool growing seasons.

directions: Titicaca was developed through a Danish university breeding program aimed at bringing quinoa into higher-latitude, shorter-summer climates where standard Andean lines fail to ripen before fall frost. It grows notably shorter and more compact than most heirloom quinoa strains, an advantage for reducing lodging in windy gardens, and its day-neutral flowering habit lets it set seed reliably regardless of daylength. Direct sow into well-drained soil in full sun and thin to a wide enough spacing for the plants to bulk up their seed heads. Cut whole plants once the seed heads dry and rattle, then thresh and rinse the harvested seed thoroughly to strip the bitter saponin coating before cooking or storing.
sources: Purdue University Center for New Crops and Plants Products

planting.note: Direct sow in early spring into well-drained soil in full sun; Black quinoa runs several weeks later to maturity than lighter-seeded quinoa strains, so give it the longest cool season available.

directions: Black quinoa produces tall seed spikes densely packed with small, glossy jet-black seed, a distinct type from the more familiar tan, red, or bicolor quinoa strains and one that takes noticeably longer to fully ripen. Its dark, tightly closed seed coat sheds moisture well, which can help it stand up to a wetter harvest window better than paler quinoa types. Grow it exactly as other quinoa: direct sow into cool spring soil, keep watering light once established since quinoa dislikes soggy roots, and stake or support plantings in windy sites given their height. Harvest whole seed heads once thoroughly dry and shattering starts, then thresh and rinse well before cooking, as the seed coat still carries the typical bitter saponin layer.
sources: Purdue University Center for New Crops and Plants Products

common_name: Tiffany Teff (Oregon State-Bred Forage and Hay Teff)

planting.note: Surface-sow the dust-fine seed after the last frost once soil has warmed; Tiffany was released by Oregon State University specifically for hay and forage production and cuts sooner than grain-type teff.

directions: Tiffany came out of an Oregon State University forage breeding effort aimed at giving Western hay growers a teff selection with better yield and stand quality than the older, unimproved teff seed lots that had been used for hay up to that point. Mix the tiny seed with sand or dry fertilizer for uniform broadcasting, then roll or cultipack the seedbed, since seed left uncovered on the surface establishes far better than seed drilled deep. It grows a fine, fibrous stand that tolerates short dry spells well and cures into a soft, palatable hay prized by horse owners for its low sugar content relative to other summer annual grasses. Cut for hay at the boot-to-early-heading stage for the best yield and quality, and expect quick regrowth for a second cutting where the season allows.

planting.note: Drill or broadcast in mid-fall so plants establish before winter dormancy; Maverick is a shorter-strawed, more lodging-resistant modern spelt widely grown by organic grain farmers as an alternative to tall heirloom lines.

directions: Maverick was bred to give organic and specialty grain growers a spelt option with a shorter, sturdier straw than older heirloom lines like Oberkulmer, cutting down on lodging losses in wet or windy years while still delivering the hulled kernel and nutty flavor spelt is grown for. Sow into a firm, well-worked seedbed in mid-fall, using a slightly heavier seeding rate than for common wheat since spelt tillers less. Plants overwinter low to the ground and resume vigorous growth in spring, typically heading out and ripening around the same window as other winter spelt lines. Because the tough hull remains fused to the kernel at harvest, plan on a dedicated dehuller or mill built for spelt rather than a standard combine setup used for free-threshing wheat.

planting.note: Sow after all danger of frost has passed and soil has warmed; Plainsman was one of the first grain amaranth selections bred specifically for reliable, comparatively early maturity in temperate US growing regions.

directions: Plainsman came out of the grain amaranth breeding work done at the Rodale Research Center in the early 1980s, part of the push to turn amaranth into a viable modern US grain crop rather than strictly a garden curiosity. It bears tan to golden upright seed heads on tall, sturdy plants and was selected in large part for maturing reliably within a single Midwestern growing season, a trait that made it a common choice in early commercial grain amaranth trial plots. Sow shallowly in warm soil once frost danger has passed, thin to a wide spacing, and let plants grow largely unattended through summer heat. Harvest once the seed heads dry and shed seed readily when rubbed between the hands, then thresh and winnow thoroughly, since amaranth seed is small and light.
sources: Purdue University Center for New Crops and Plants Products

planting.note: Broadcast or drill into warm soil once all frost danger has passed; Pennquad is a chromosome-doubled tetraploid buckwheat bred at Penn State for larger milling seed and is killed outright by the lightest freeze.

directions: Pennquad was created at Pennsylvania State University by chemically doubling the chromosome number of ordinary buckwheat, a tetraploid conversion that yields noticeably larger, heavier groats better suited to milling for flour and whole-grain use than standard diploid buckwheat. The tradeoff for that bigger seed is a lower seed set per plant and thicker, somewhat more brittle stems that can lodge more readily in heavy rain or wind, so it rewards a well-drained site with modest fertility rather than a rich one. Drill or broadcast into a warm, well-worked seedbed after the last frost, and expect the dense white bloom to draw pollinators heavily during its several-week flowering window. Mow or turn it under at first bloom for cover-crop use, or let it stand to full seed maturity and dry down if growing it for grain harvest.
sources: Pennsylvania State University Department of Plant Science
